title: Battleborn
text: I mean, it's not like it's awful. Battleborn is not Overwatch. They are barely similar. One is a first person MOBA, the other is a hero based arena shooter. That being said, I'm not here to argue which is better. You shouldn't play Battleborn though, unless you want a tedious 8-ish hour single player campaign. The multiplayer is nonexistant, so I literally could not play it other than with bots. It has some interesting concepts and it seems to translate pretty well from your DOTA/League to a first person format. The rest of this will just be about the single player. You level your character between two options, and you redo this every mission. Some characters have upgrades that funtamentally change how they play, like the DLC lizard assassin man, who you can turn into a glass vampire instead of being a DOT dealer. However, others have basic stat buffs and such, and are pretty boring as a result. The robot sniper is just that, buffs and casting ranges. You go up to level 10, and that seems like not much, but the levels drag out to DOTA lengths. Each level is what you would think. Go to A, defend B for three waves, move to C, defend D for three waves. It's super boring a lot of the time. All the time, actually. The color palette for each level is also the same throughout the whole thing. There is no visual variety, making even looking at the game a chore. Enemies all practically act the same; rush and hit you, stay back and shoot you, throw things at you, or spawn enemies to do the first three. They don't dodge or coordinate at all. Right before each mission starts, the same unskippable poorly animated animation plays, and it lasts around thirty seconds. Or it at least feels that long. There is a gear system which is super bizzare to me. You find gear in the levels either in chests (that function identically to Borderlands) or get them off bosses. You then have to go back to the main menu and open up the gear to see what you actually get. After this, you equip it, and have to go in game to unlock it for that mission with the in game currency that you only earn for that level. This applies to the multiplayer as well. The gear is only just stat boosts with some occasional downsides. Just stat decreases. Optimization is poor. Even Borderlands ran badly. I have a 1070 and a 1500x, and sometimes I drop to 50 when looking somewhat far away. It's not acceptable, especially after so long. Battleborn isn't even graphically impressive. It looks like an early 7th gen game through and through. And yet, I don't even mind it. I finished the story, even though it was terrible, the writing was laughable, and the cartoon animations are DeviantArt levels of unfinished, unpolished and just annoying. I think the gunplay is just solid. Melee characters are usually really interesting to play as, especially the lizard man previously mentioned. I can't really explain what compelled me to finish it, but I don't think it's the worst thing ever made. Not like Randy Pitchford's live performance of his original song. Try it for cheap. Like, real cheap. Ten Americabucks at most.

title: Beyond Eyes
text: Walking Simulators, are games that are in my wheelhouse. They are usually short, so I can beat it in one session; they usually tell a story - compelling or not is decision based on player to player basis of course; and indie developers try to put their soul and hard work, to bring us to their world and show us something new, give us some new experiences. And 'New Experience' is exactly how I would define . From start, we are in this unusual setting. We play as Rae - little girl who is sadly blind. And this idea, is original for me. I never encounter game with this concept; and I have to say it is masterfully executed. In terms of visual feedback, sounds, you as a player feel somewhat uncomfortable because you can't see where you going, and even now I can hardly imagine how hard have to be for people who are blind, to deal with this. At least we get some visual feedback, instead of pitch black darkness. In this way I feel is absolutely great, and when you add piano into your soundtrack, I am sold. On the other hand. Levels tend to drag for a little bit, and after half and hour, I wasn't that much interested to explore every corner, every direction of my journey. I was only focused on the road ahead of me, with one and only goal - finish this game. If the game is two hour long, those two hours should be filled every now and then, with something more valuable then constant white screen, plants, trees, water ... maybe more encounters either pleasant or scary to make things more interesting, and feel that this world is more alive. I think that would help us, to understand how blind people, especially kids, think about world, how their imagination works, which in the end would add more emotions to the game if we would be able to see happiness or despair in more moments. Also, theme of anxiety would maybe get more shine, and would be more visible, thanks to more events and more realistic events. I do recommend to play , because game has a new approach,  doesn't play safe and it's taking chances - which I feel could be ballsier.

title: Beyond Eyes
text: Beyond Eyes set out to accomplish a lofty goal, create a game that would give the player a taste of what it would be like to go blind.  Not only did it accomplish this goal via very creative game concepts, but it tells a simple and endearing yarn of a blind child in search of her feline friend that really made me feel for the main character, Rae. From a technical standpoint the gameplay is simply walking and exploring, but as you can imagine walking and exploring without sight would be anything but simple.  Beyond Eyes world is beautifully colored and rendered, think watercolor painting, but most of it is shrouded in white except for your near vicinity.  As you move thru the landscape your world literally pops into existence out of the white, often with annoying reality like a fence right where you are trying to walk.  Sound is a key part of the experience too, not only in the stellar game audio but in distant visual bubble that becomes a beacon in the unknown for Rae to navigate towards.  Smell is also represented visually by wind waves, but be warned, both smell and sound can be misleading. Beyond Eyes not only gave me a “glimpse” into the world of a blind person, but it succeeded in making me feel for Rae.  The frustration of another dead end, the confusion of thinking you hear or smell something interesting that turns out to be something completely different, the sadness of loss, the joy of succeeding at simple tasks previously taken for granted.  Beyond Eyes requires patience, empathy and a sense of exploration, but will reward you with a one of a kind experience and a charming fairytale that will stick with you long after playing.

However I do have one huge gripe with the game outside of the graphics options. In the game, hacking is a decently essential tool in your arsenal. Having access to certain defences, unlocking safes with valuable resources and even getting a better price on your favorite ammunition can be crucial in winning on the harder difficulties with ease. When I say all sides were covered I mean there was a 0% chance of successfully completing the hack because there was no where for the liquid to go, on every single side it would have hit a dead end, and those tiles cant be moved so it was either failing the hack or hitting one of them and getting dicked over just for wanting to open a safe. This issue should have been fixed when the game first came out because it has done this since the games release, before any sequels were made and before a remastered edition was probably even conceived. title: Bionic Commando: Rearmed
text: I came here with the purpose of finding a game I didn't like and seeing if it was worth a negative review. Glad I came back to this one.  As it turns out, its a rough diamond. Its a jarring game to play initially.  We are so used to knowing what a shooter is and what a platformer is.  When a game like Bionic Commando denies us a jump button then it becomes very stressful.  My advice is do the tutorials and attempt the challenge rooms within the friendly zones first. They will teach you the mechanics and you will quickly be able to move fluidly the way you want to and be a true bionic commando, instead of a slow clunky frustrated commando wondering what you are doing. The swing mechanics of the bionic arm are very fun once you take a few minutes to get used to them, and you will be taking on platforms and bad guys with ease quickly.  You won't even mind not having a jump button after you've figured it all out. Level progression is a bit different too.  Area 0 is a friendly zone that must be entered to find the tutorial, and Area 1 must be entered to find the challenge rooms that put into practice more of the advanced skills. You won't initially know where to go, but by exploring the areas you can access you will eventually build up a handy arsenal of equipment and knowledge of the game.   I highly recommend exploring all the friendly zone to start with and entering the rooms to collect useful equipment as well as getting used to moving around outside of combat.  After you've comfortably explored the friendly areas and rooms, tackle the nearby accessable low numbered areas and dominate those enemies in combat. As an example of a time where you will be initially confused, you need to explore a friendly zone to get the flares you need to more easily explore Area 4.  The level can still possibly be completed, but you will get frustrated wondering why an early level has you zipping about blind trying to find a random platform or bit of wall you need to succeed.  Turns out exploration of a friendly zone was the answer and only one I discovered by accident after getting frustrated and quitting out to try another stage. Bosses are in every enemy stage, and there is a great mechanic where you can hack enemy consoles for a chance of learning the boss weakness.  I found the early bosses to be easy enough that I didn't get frustrated and wanted to keep playing.  Beating bosses earns you more gear as well as more levels to play with so its a rewarding experience. There are also enemy trucks zipping about the world map also give you a chance to play a different kind of shooting game and experiment with weapons.  Its a bit repetitive, but a fun distraction between the main game. In conclusion, Bionic Commando Rearmed is definitely a game that tries something different and succeeds.  If you can cope with it being different, put in that half an hour to learn how to play the game.  There is a real treat lying ahead for you. EDIT: I'll admit later levels and challenges do become frustrating so just enjoy the fun bits.

title: Bionic Commando: Rearmed
text: I wanted to like this game but it is killed by the same crappy control scheme that the original NES version was infamous for. Back in those NES glory days, we kids never questioned why a bionic commando would be unable to jump or climb over an obstacle. Now, though, it’s stupid and frustrating. Many positive reviews celebrate this as being a “hard” game, but all of its difficulty stems from the crappy controls. It shouldn’t be rewarded for bad design. I could get over not being able to jump or climb if the grappling mechanics were smooth and responsive, but they aren’t. They’re clunky & counter intuitive. And this in a game full of instant death areas that oh by the way gives you a certain number of lives to get through each level. I stopped this after about an hour, once I reached a level with a secret area I could not get into after dying & starting all the way over five times. I knew exactly what I had to do and it wasn’t very complicated, but the controls are so unresponsive it became impossibly hard. Then I thought about how, if I did manage to make it into the secret area, I would have to navigate back out the way I came and survive through the rest of the level and the boss fight. If I ran out of lives before that, I’d have to do the entire level all over again. Who thinks that’s fun? This game could have been great if they had retooled the grappling system and the level designs. Instead they essentially lifted everything straight from the NES original aside from the graphics. If they weren’t going to update the controls, they should have at least given infinite lives & checkpoints inside levels since the gameplay boils down to tons of trial, error & luck. I bought this during a Steam sale and I regret the purchase. My advice is to get an emulated version of the original NES version. It will give you almost the same experience.
